paragraphs: The fairer opponents of the provision on elections contained in the plan of the Convention will sometimes, when pressed in argument, concede that the provision is proper. They add this qualification, however: it ought to have been accompanied by a declaration that all elections should be held in the counties where the electors reside. This, they say, was a necessary precaution against abuse of the power. A declaration of this nature would certainly have been harmless, and so far as it would have quieted apprehensions it might not have been undesirable. But it would in fact have given little or no additional security against the danger feared. An impartial and judicious examiner will never regard its absence as a serious objection to the plan, still less as an insuperable one. The different views taken of the subject in the two preceding papers must be enough to satisfy all dispassionate and discerning men that if public liberty should ever fall victim to the ambition of the national rulers, the power under examination, at least, will be guiltless of the sacrifice.

If those who are inclined to consult only their jealousy would exercise it in a careful inspection of the individual State constitutions, they would find little less cause for uneasiness and alarm in the latitude most of them allow with respect to elections than in the latitude proposed to be allowed to the national government in the same respect. A review of their situation in this particular would do much to remove any ill impressions that may remain on this matter. But as that review would lead into long and tedious details, I shall content myself with the single example of the State in which I write. The constitution of New York makes no other provision for the LOCALITY of elections than that the members of the Assembly shall be elected in the COUNTIES, and those of the Senate in the great districts into which the State is or may be divided. At present these are four in number, and each comprehends from two to six counties. It may readily be seen that it would be no more difficult for the legislature of New York to defeat the votes of the citizens of New York by confining elections to particular places than for the legislature of the United States to defeat the votes of the citizens of the Union by the same expedient. Suppose, for instance, that the city of Albany were appointed the sole place of election for the county and district of which it is a part. Would not the inhabitants of that city soon become the only electors of the members of both the Senate and the Assembly for that county and district? Can we imagine that the electors living in the remote subdivisions of the counties of Albany, Saratoga, Cambridge and so on, or in any part of the county of Montgomery, would take the trouble to come to the city of Albany to vote for members of the Assembly or Senate, sooner than they would travel to the city of New York to take part in choosing the members of the federal House of Representatives? The alarming indifference to be seen in the exercise of so invaluable a privilege under the existing laws, which make every facility available for it, gives a ready answer to this question. And, setting aside any experience on the subject, we can have no difficulty in determining that when the place of election is at an INCONVENIENT DISTANCE from the elector, the effect on his conduct will be the same whether that distance is twenty miles or twenty thousand miles. Hence it must be clear that objections to the particular arrangement of the federal power to regulate elections apply in substance with equal force to the arrangement of the like power in the constitution of this State. For this reason it will be impossible to acquit the one and condemn the other. A similar comparison would lead to the same conclusion about the constitutions of most of the other States.

If it should be said that defects in the State constitutions furnish no excuse for those found in the proposed plan, I answer as follows. The former have never been thought chargeable with inattention to the security of liberty. Where the accusations thrown at the latter can be shown to apply to them also, the presumption is that those accusations are rather the petty quibbles of a predetermined opposition than the well-founded inferences of a fair search after truth. To those who are disposed to regard as innocent omissions in the State constitutions what they regard as unpardonable blemishes in the plan of the Convention, nothing can be said. At most they can only be asked to give some substantial reason why the representatives of the people in a single State should be more impregnable to the lust of power or to other sinister motives than the representatives of the people of the United States. If they cannot do this, they ought at least to prove to us that it is easier to subvert the liberties of three million people, with the advantage of local governments to head their opposition, than those of two hundred thousand people who lack that advantage. And with respect to the point immediately under consideration, they ought to convince us that it is less probable for a predominant faction in a single State to lean, in order to maintain its superiority, toward a preference for a particular class of electors than for a similar spirit to take possession of the representatives of thirteen States, spread over a vast region and distinguished from each other in several respects by a diversity of local circumstances, prejudices and interests.

So far my observations have aimed only at vindicating the provision in question on the ground of theoretical propriety, on the ground of the danger of placing the power elsewhere, and on the ground of the safety of placing it in the manner proposed. But there remains to be mentioned a positive advantage that will result from this arrangement, and that could not as well have been obtained from any other. I refer to the uniformity in the time of elections for the federal House of Representatives. It is more than possible that experience will show this uniformity to be of great importance to the public welfare, both as a security against the perpetuation of the same spirit in the body and as a cure for the diseases of faction. If each State may choose its own time of election, there may possibly be as many different times as there are months in the year. The times of election in the individual States, as they are now established for local purposes, vary between extremes as far apart as March and November. The consequence of this diversity would be that there could never be a total dissolution or renewal of the body at one time. If an improper spirit of any kind should happen to prevail in it, that spirit would be apt to infuse itself into the new members as they came in one after another. The mass would be likely to remain nearly the same, constantly assimilating to itself its gradual additions. There is a contagion in example that few men have strength of mind enough to resist. I am inclined to think that three times the duration in office, on condition that the whole body is dissolved at the same time, might be less formidable to liberty than one third of that duration subject to gradual and successive changes.
Uniformity in the time of elections seems no less necessary for carrying out the idea of a regular rotation in the Senate, and for conveniently assembling the legislature at a fixed time each year.

It may be asked why, then, a time could not have been fixed in the Constitution. Since the most zealous adversaries of the plan of the Convention in this State are, in general, no less zealous admirers of the State constitution, the question may be turned back on them: why was no time fixed for the like purpose in the constitution of this State? No better answer can be given than that it was a matter which could safely be entrusted to legislative discretion, and that if a time had been appointed, it might, on trial, have proved less convenient than some other time. The same answer may be given to the question put on the other side. It may be added that, since the supposed danger of a gradual change is merely speculative, it would hardly have been advisable, on the strength of that speculation, to establish as a fundamental point something that would deprive several States of the convenience of having the elections for their own governments and for the national government at the same times.
